subChunks.title: Aggregate Functions — COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX
subChunks.hookHtml: So far every query has returned rows. Sometimes you don't want rows — you want a summary. "How many apprentices?" "What's the total XP awarded?" "What's the highest grade?" These collapse a whole column into one number. The five functions that do it are COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The five aggregate functions

FunctionMeaningType
COUNT(*)How many rowsWorks on any table
COUNT(col)How many non-NULL values in colAny column
SUM(col)Total of all valuesNumeric only
AVG(col)Average valueNumeric only
MIN(col)Smallest valueNumeric, text, or date
MAX(col)Largest valueNumeric, text, or date

The shape of an aggregate query

-- How many apprentices in total?
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM apprentices;

-- Highest XP among all apprentices:
SELECT MAX(xp) FROM apprentices;

-- Total XP across all apprentices:
SELECT SUM(xp) FROM apprentices;

-- Average XP:
SELECT AVG(xp) FROM apprentices;

Each query returns a single row, single column. The whole table collapses into one number.

The COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) distinction

This trips everyone up at first.

-- COUNT(*) — every row, regardless of NULLs:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM quests;          -- 5

-- COUNT(column) — rows where that column is NOT NULL:
SELECT COUNT(completed_by) FROM quests;  -- 3
--   (rows 1, 2, 5 have completed_by; rows 3, 4 are NULL)

-- COUNT(DISTINCT column) — distinct non-NULL values:
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT difficulty) FROM quests;  -- 3
--   (Foundation, Practitioner, Expert)

Use COUNT(*) when you want "how many rows." Use COUNT(col) when you want "how many rows have a value in this column." Use COUNT(DISTINCT col) when you want "how many unique values."

NULL is invisible to aggregates (except COUNT(*))

Aggregates skip NULLs:

-- If quests has 5 rows and 2 have NULL difficulty,
-- AVG only divides by 3, not 5.
SELECT AVG(xp_reward) FROM quests;

This is usually what you want — averaging zero-where-actually-unknown would skew results. But it means SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX may quietly ignore data you didn't realise was missing. Always check whether NULLs are meaningful in your dataset.

Combine with WHERE for filtered aggregates

-- Average XP among Mages only:
SELECT AVG(xp) FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Mage';

-- Number of Foundation quests with rewards over 100:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM quests
WHERE difficulty = 'Foundation' AND xp_reward > 100;

WHERE filters first, the aggregate runs over what's left. Same precedence as before: SELECT, FROM, WHERE — and now the SELECT clause contains an aggregate function.

Naming the result

Aggregate columns get ugly default names like count(*). Rename with AS for tidy output:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_apprentices,
       AVG(xp) AS mean_xp,
       MAX(xp) AS top_xp
FROM apprentices;

storyBeats.text: Cipher dusts a heavy black ledger and lays it open. The first page is blank — except for a single number written in red ink at the top right corner.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: The Headmaster reads summaries. He doesn't want to see every row. He wants one number. Total XP awarded last term. Average grade. Number of apprentices in each rank. The shape of his question is not 'show me data' — it is 'collapse the data into one figure.'

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: There are five workhorses. COUNT — how many. SUM — total. AVG — average. MIN and MAX — smallest and largest. Each one takes a column and gives back a single value. The whole ledger boils down to a single cell.

storyBeats.speaker: Five summaries of the apprentices ledger
storyBeats.text:
SELECT COUNT(*)  AS num_apprentices,
       SUM(xp)   AS total_xp,
       AVG(xp)   AS mean_xp,
       MIN(xp)   AS lowest_xp,
       MAX(xp)   AS highest_xp
FROM apprentices;

-- Result, given our four-row ledger:
-- num_apprentices | total_xp | mean_xp | lowest_xp | highest_xp
-- ----------------+----------+---------+-----------+-----------
--        4        |   8480   |  2120.0 |    80     |   4800

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: And one trap: COUNT(*) counts every row. COUNT(column_name) counts only rows where that column is not NULL. If half your completed_by values are NULL, COUNT(completed_by) will be smaller than COUNT(*) — and that's usually the truth you want, but only if you remember to ask for it correctly.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Aggregates are also where NULL becomes useful, in a way. AVG, SUM, MIN, MAX all skip NULL values automatically. So if a column has 100 entries and 30 are NULL, the average divides by 70, not 100. Whether that's the right answer depends on what NULL means in your data. Check, every time.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
🪄 Summary statistics

The Headmaster wants three numbers in one row from the apprentices table:

  • Total number of apprentices, aliased num_apprentices
  • Sum of all XP, aliased total_xp
  • The highest XP value, aliased top_xp

One query, one row, three columns. Use AS to rename each aggregate.

Reference data:

id | name    | rank        | xp
---+---------+-------------+------

 2 | Bjorn   | Adept       | 2400
 3 | Cassia  | Mage        | 4800
 4 | Dorian  | Novice      |   80

Expected single-row result: num_apprentices=4, total_xp=8480, top_xp=4800.

-- One row, three aggregate columns.
SELECT
  -- COUNT(*)  AS num_apprentices,
  -- SUM(xp)   AS total_xp,
  -- MAX(xp)   AS top_xp
FROM apprentices;

guidedPracticeTests.setup: CREATE TABLE apprentices (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, rank TEXT NOT NULL, xp INTEGER NOT NULL); INSERT INTO apprentices VALUES (1,'Alice','Apprentice',1200),(2,'Bjorn','Adept',2400),(3,'Cassia','Mage',4800),(4,'Dorian','Novice',80);

🏹 Solo Challenge — Mage stats

Same data. Write a query that returns the average XP among Mages only. One row, one column called mage_avg. Hint: combine AVG() with a WHERE clause.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between COUNT(*), COUNT(column), and COUNT(DISTINCT column). Use the quests table to give a concrete value for each, and explain why a junior who writes COUNT(completed_by) might be surprised by the result.

questions.questionHtml: What does SUM(xp) return when applied to the apprentices table?
options: The arithmetic sum of every non-NULL xp value
The number of apprentices
The largest xp value
The smallest xp value
questions.correctAnswer: The arithmetic sum of every non-NULL xp value
questions.explanationHtml: SUM totals the values, skipping NULL. COUNT counts rows. MIN and MAX return the smallest and largest values respectively.

questions.questionHtml:
Using the quests table from the lesson (5 rows, 2 NULL difficulties, 2 NULL completed_by), what does this return?

SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(completed_by), COUNT(DISTINCT difficulty) FROM quests;
questions.explanationHtml: COUNT(*) = 5 rows total. COUNT(completed_by) = 3 (rows 3 and 4 are NULL). COUNT(DISTINCT difficulty) = 3 (Foundation, Practitioner, Expert — NULL is not a distinct value for COUNT DISTINCT).

questions.questionHtml: Which query returns the highest xp among Adepts?
options: SELECT MAX(xp) FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Adept';
SELECT TOP(xp) FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Adept';
SELECT xp FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Adept' AND xp = MAX;
SELECT MAX(rank) FROM apprentices WHERE xp = 'Adept';
questions.correctAnswer: SELECT MAX(xp) FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Adept';
questions.explanationHtml: WHERE filters to Adepts; MAX(xp) collapses the remaining rows into a single largest-xp value. The other forms either use non-existent functions or compare wrong columns.

questions.questionHtml: Two queries claim to find "the average XP of all completed quests." Which one is correct, given that completed_by is NULL when nobody has completed the quest?
options: SELECT AVG(xp_reward) FROM quests WHERE completed_by IS NOT NULL;
SELECT AVG(xp_reward) FROM quests WHERE completed_by != NULL;
SELECT AVG(xp_reward) FROM quests;
SELECT COUNT(xp_reward) / COUNT(*) FROM quests;
questions.correctAnswer: SELECT AVG(xp_reward) FROM quests WHERE completed_by IS NOT NULL;
questions.explanationHtml: Option 1 is correct. Option 2 fails because != NULL never matches anything (you must use IS NOT NULL). Option 3 averages over all quests including unfinished ones — wrong scope. Option 4 computes the ratio of non-NULL rewards to total rows, which is a different statistic entirely (it's the fraction of quests with a defined reward).

subChunks.title: GROUP BY — Aggregating per-bucket
subChunks.hookHtml: One number is good. One number per category is better. "Total XP" is interesting; "total XP per rank" tells you which tier of the Academy is doing the most work. GROUP BY is what turns a single summary into a per-bucket breakdown — and once you internalise it, half of all SQL queries fall into place.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The mental model

GROUP BY column tells SQL: "divide the rows into buckets where every row in a bucket has the same value of column. Then run the aggregate functions within each bucket."

-- One row per rank, with a count + average xp per rank:
SELECT rank,
       COUNT(*)  AS num_apprentices,
       AVG(xp)   AS mean_xp
FROM apprentices
GROUP BY rank;

-- Result, given our 4-row table:
-- rank        | num_apprentices | mean_xp
-- ------------+-----------------+--------
-- Apprentice  |       1         |  1200
-- Adept       |       1         |  2400
-- Mage        |       1         |  4800
-- Novice      |       1         |    80

The rule that catches everyone

When you use GROUP BY, every column in the SELECT list must either be:

  • Listed in the GROUP BY clause, OR
  • Wrapped in an aggregate function

This won't work in PostgreSQL or in standard SQL:

-- ERROR — `name` is neither grouped nor aggregated:
SELECT rank, name, COUNT(*) FROM apprentices GROUP BY rank;

Why? Each rank-bucket may contain many rows, each with a different name. SQL doesn't know which name to pick. (MySQL with default settings will silently pick an arbitrary one — a footgun. Other engines throw an error.)

Either group by name too:

SELECT rank, name, COUNT(*) FROM apprentices GROUP BY rank, name;

… or aggregate it (e.g. STRING_AGG(name, ', ')) — though that's an advanced move.

Multi-column GROUP BY

-- One row per (difficulty, completion-status) combination:
SELECT difficulty,
       (completed_by IS NOT NULL) AS finished,
       COUNT(*) AS num_quests
FROM quests
GROUP BY difficulty, finished;

The bucket key is the tuple of grouped columns. Two rows are in the same bucket only if they match on every grouped column.

WHERE happens before GROUP BY

-- Average xp per rank, restricted to apprentices with non-zero xp:
SELECT rank, AVG(xp) AS mean_xp
FROM apprentices
WHERE xp > 0
GROUP BY rank;

Pipeline: WHERE filters → GROUP BY buckets → aggregates compute. Filtering happens first, on raw rows. To filter after aggregation (e.g. "only ranks where the count is > 1"), you need HAVING — next sub-chunk.

The full clause order, revised

SELECT <columns and aggregates>
FROM <table>
WHERE <row-level condition>
GROUP BY <bucket columns>
ORDER BY <sort columns>
LIMIT <n>;

WHERE filters rows. GROUP BY makes buckets. ORDER BY sorts the result rows. LIMIT trims. Always in that sequence.

storyBeats.text: Cipher unrolls a fresh sheet of parchment and ink-stamps a heading: 'XP per rank.'

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: The Headmaster's question is no longer 'how many apprentices?' but 'how many apprentices at each rank?' We are no longer collapsing to a single number — we are producing one number per category. This is what GROUP BY does.

storyBeats.speaker: Per-rank summary
storyBeats.text:
SELECT rank,
       COUNT(*) AS num_apprentices,
       AVG(xp)  AS mean_xp
FROM apprentices
GROUP BY rank;

-- One row per distinct rank value:
-- rank        | num_apprentices | mean_xp
-- ------------+-----------------+--------
-- Apprentice  |       1         |  1200
-- Adept       |       1         |  2400
-- Mage        |       1         |  4800
-- Novice      |       1         |    80

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: The rule you must internalise: every column in the SELECT list is either in the GROUP BY clause, or wrapped in an aggregate. Nothing else is allowed. SELECT rank, name, COUNT(*) FROM apprentices GROUP BY rank is nonsense — for a given rank-bucket there are many possible names, so which one would the engine pick? Standard SQL refuses to choose.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Picture it as physically sorting the rows into piles. One pile per distinct value of the GROUP BY columns. Then for each pile you compute one summary row — that's what comes out. If a column varies inside a pile, the engine has no single answer to give for it. Either include it in the bucketing, or aggregate it.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
🪄 Quest count per difficulty

The Headmaster wants one row per difficulty, with the count of quests in each. Filter out the NULL-difficulty quest first — it's a known data-entry mistake.

  • Two columns: difficulty and num_quests (COUNT(*) aliased)
  • Filter difficulty IS NOT NULL in WHERE
  • Group by difficulty

Reference data:

id | title              | xp_reward | difficulty   | completed_by
---+--------------------+-----------+--------------+--------------
 1 | Tame the Slime     |   100     | Foundation   | 1
 2 | Decode the Glyph   |   180     | Foundation   | 2
 3 | Forge the Blade    |   400     | Practitioner | NULL
 4 | Slay the Drake     |  1200     | Expert       | NULL
 5 | Brew the Elixir    |   220     | NULL         | 3

Expected: Foundation=2, Practitioner=1, Expert=1.
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
-- One row per difficulty, with the count.
-- Drop the NULL-difficulty row first.
SELECT difficulty, COUNT(*) AS num_quests
FROM quests
WHERE
  -- only non-NULL difficulties
GROUP BY
  -- ?
;

guidedPracticeTests.label: Returns 3 rows (one per non-NULL difficulty)
guidedPracticeTests.setup: CREATE TABLE quests (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL, xp_reward INTEGER NOT NULL, difficulty TEXT, completed_by INTEGER); INSERT INTO quests VALUES (1,'Tame the Slime',100,'Foundation',1),(2,'Decode the Glyph',180,'Foundation',2),(3,'Forge the Blade',400,'Practitioner',NULL),(4,'Slay the Drake',1200,'Expert',NULL),(5,'Brew the Elixir',220,NULL,3);

guidedPracticeTests.expectedQuery: SELECT difficulty, COUNT(*) AS num_quests FROM quests WHERE difficulty IS NOT NULL GROUP BY difficulty

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo Challenge — Total XP per difficulty

Same data. Write a query that returns one row per non-NULL difficulty, with the total xp_reward across that difficulty's quests. Columns: difficulty and total_reward. Use SUM.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why the query 'SELECT rank, name, COUNT(*) FROM apprentices GROUP BY rank' is invalid in standard SQL. Walk through what each rank-bucket would contain and why there is no sensible value for 'name' in the result row.

options: Divides the rows into buckets by rank, then runs aggregates per bucket
Sorts the result by rank
Removes duplicate rank values
Filters rows where rank is NULL
questions.correctAnswer: Divides the rows into buckets by rank, then runs aggregates per bucket
questions.explanationHtml: GROUP BY produces one output row per distinct combination of grouped values. Aggregates in the SELECT clause run within each bucket. ORDER BY does sorting; DISTINCT does deduplication; WHERE / IS NULL handle filtering.

questions.questionHtml:
Using the quests table, what does this query return?

SELECT difficulty, COUNT(*) AS num
FROM quests
GROUP BY difficulty;
options: Foundation 2, Practitioner 1, Expert 1, NULL 1
Foundation 2, Practitioner 1, Expert 1 (the NULL row is silently dropped)
Foundation, Practitioner, Expert (one row each, no counts)
5 (single number — total quests)
questions.explanationHtml: GROUP BY does not drop NULL values — they form their own bucket. So you get four buckets: Foundation (2 rows), Practitioner (1), Expert (1), and NULL (1, for Brew the Elixir). This surprises many newcomers.

questions.questionHtml:
Why does this query fail in PostgreSQL?

SELECT difficulty, title, COUNT(*)
FROM quests
GROUP BY difficulty;
options: title is neither in the GROUP BY clause nor wrapped in an aggregate, so the engine has no single value to pick per bucket
COUNT(*) can only appear with one other column in SELECT
GROUP BY must always include every column in the SELECT list, even those wrapped in aggregates
title is a reserved word
questions.correctAnswer: title is neither in the GROUP BY clause nor wrapped in an aggregate, so the engine has no single value to pick per bucket
questions.explanationHtml: This is the canonical GROUP BY rule: every non-aggregated column in SELECT must appear in GROUP BY. Each bucket has multiple rows with potentially different titles — the engine refuses to pick one arbitrarily. (MySQL with default settings will pick an arbitrary one, which is a notorious footgun.)

questions.questionHtml: You want "average xp_reward per difficulty, but only counting quests that have been completed." Which query is correct?
options: SELECT difficulty, AVG(xp_reward) FROM quests WHERE completed_by IS NOT NULL GROUP BY difficulty;
SELECT difficulty, AVG(xp_reward) FROM quests GROUP BY difficulty WHERE completed_by IS NOT NULL;
SELECT difficulty, AVG(xp_reward) FROM quests GROUP BY difficulty AND completed_by IS NOT NULL;
SELECT difficulty, AVG(xp_reward) FROM quests HAVING completed_by IS NOT NULL GROUP BY difficulty;
questions.correctAnswer: SELECT difficulty, AVG(xp_reward) FROM quests WHERE completed_by IS NOT NULL GROUP BY difficulty;
questions.explanationHtml: WHERE filters rows before grouping — exactly what we want here (drop unfinished quests, then bucket what's left). The other forms either put WHERE in the wrong position (syntax error), use AND inside GROUP BY (syntax error), or misuse HAVING (HAVING filters buckets, not rows — covered next sub-chunk).

subChunks.title: HAVING — Filtering Buckets
subChunks.hookHtml: WHERE filters rows. GROUP BY makes buckets. HAVING filters buckets. Once you internalise the difference between row-level conditions and bucket-level conditions, the entire SQL clause-ordering puzzle clicks into place.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The full pipeline

Every SELECT query runs in this conceptual order:

  1. FROM — pick the source rows
  2. WHERE — drop rows that don't match a row-level condition
  3. GROUP BY — divide remaining rows into buckets
  4. HAVING — drop buckets whose summary doesn't match a bucket-level condition
  5. SELECT — project the result columns + aggregates
  6. ORDER BY — sort the output
  7. LIMIT — cap the number of result rows

You write them in the order SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT. The engine evaluates them in the order above. The mismatch is what makes SQL feel weird at first; once you internalise it, queries become trivial to read.

HAVING — the canonical example

-- One row per rank, but ONLY ranks with more than one apprentice:
SELECT rank, COUNT(*) AS num
FROM apprentices
GROUP BY rank
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

You cannot use WHERE COUNT(*) > 1 for this — WHERE runs on individual rows, before any aggregation has happened. There is no count yet for WHERE to compare against. HAVING runs after grouping, when each bucket has its summary computed.

WHERE vs HAVING — the distinction

-- WHERE: drop rows BEFORE grouping (filter raw quests)
SELECT difficulty, AVG(xp_reward)
FROM quests
WHERE difficulty IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY difficulty;

-- HAVING: drop buckets AFTER grouping (filter difficulty groups
--         by their group-level statistic)
SELECT difficulty, AVG(xp_reward) AS mean
FROM quests
GROUP BY difficulty
HAVING AVG(xp_reward) > 200;

You can use both in one query. WHERE drops rows that aren't worth bucketing in the first place; HAVING drops buckets that don't satisfy a post-aggregation condition.

HAVING without GROUP BY

It's legal but unusual. With no GROUP BY, the entire table is one implicit bucket, and HAVING decides whether to return that single summary row.

-- Returns one row only if the average is over 1000:
SELECT AVG(xp) FROM apprentices HAVING AVG(xp) > 1000;

You'll see this rarely in practice — but knowing it's allowed prevents confusion when you encounter it.

Putting it all together

SELECT difficulty,
       COUNT(*)         AS num_quests,
       AVG(xp_reward)   AS mean_reward
FROM quests
WHERE difficulty IS NOT NULL                  -- drop the NULL-difficulty row
GROUP BY difficulty                            -- bucket by difficulty
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2                          -- only difficulties with 2+ quests
ORDER BY mean_reward DESC                      -- highest-mean first
LIMIT 5;                                       -- top 5 max

Read it as a pipeline: rows flow in, get filtered, bucketed, the buckets get filtered, the surviving buckets get projected, sorted, and capped. Every clause has a precise role in that flow.

storyBeats.text: Cipher pushes back from the desk and stretches. The afternoon light has shifted across the Hall.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Two filters, not one. Most apprentices don't notice the difference for years. WHERE filters rows — individual records. HAVING filters buckets — groups, after they've been formed and summarised. They look superficially the same. They are not. Mistaking one for the other is the second-most-common SQL bug, after the = NULL trap.

storyBeats.speaker: WHERE vs HAVING
storyBeats.text:
-- WRONG — WHERE COUNT(*) is meaningless;
-- WHERE runs before COUNT exists.
SELECT rank, COUNT(*)
FROM apprentices
WHERE COUNT(*) > 1
GROUP BY rank;          -- ERROR

-- RIGHT — HAVING runs after grouping.
SELECT rank, COUNT(*)
FROM apprentices
GROUP BY rank
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Think of it as two filters at two different stations. WHERE is the gate at the entrance — it decides which rows even enter the room. GROUP BY then sorts the survivors into stalls. HAVING is the inspector who walks past the stalls afterwards and ejects the ones whose summary doesn't qualify.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: And the order on the parchment is fixed: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT. You can't put HAVING before GROUP BY, or WHERE after it. The engine will refuse to read the page. Memorise the order — and remember that the engine evaluates them in a different order than they appear, which is exactly the asymmetry that makes the language confusing for the first month.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
🪄 The full pipeline

The Headmaster wants only the difficulties where the average reward is over 200 XP, and for each, both the count of quests and the average reward.

  • Filter NULL difficulties out via WHERE first
  • Group by difficulty
  • Filter buckets via HAVING AVG(xp_reward) > 200
  • Three columns: difficulty, num_quests (COUNT(*) aliased), mean_reward (AVG(xp_reward) aliased)

Reference data:

id | title              | xp_reward | difficulty   | completed_by
---+--------------------+-----------+--------------+--------------
 1 | Tame the Slime     |   100     | Foundation   | 1
 2 | Decode the Glyph   |   180     | Foundation   | 2
 3 | Forge the Blade    |   400     | Practitioner | NULL
 4 | Slay the Drake     |  1200     | Expert       | NULL
 5 | Brew the Elixir    |   220     | NULL         | 3

Expected: Foundation has avg=140 (excluded), Practitioner has avg=400 (included), Expert has avg=1200 (included). Result: 2 rows.
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
-- Difficulty buckets where average reward > 200.
SELECT difficulty,
       COUNT(*)       AS num_quests,
       AVG(xp_reward) AS mean_reward
FROM quests
WHERE
  -- difficulty IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY difficulty
HAVING
  -- AVG(xp_reward) > 200
;

guidedPracticeTests.label: Returns 2 rows (Practitioner and Expert)
guidedPracticeTests.setup: CREATE TABLE quests (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL, xp_reward INTEGER NOT NULL, difficulty TEXT, completed_by INTEGER); INSERT INTO quests VALUES (1,'Tame the Slime',100,'Foundation',1),(2,'Decode the Glyph',180,'Foundation',2),(3,'Forge the Blade',400,'Practitioner',NULL),(4,'Slay the Drake',1200,'Expert',NULL),(5,'Brew the Elixir',220,NULL,3);

guidedPracticeTests.label: Practitioner (1, 400) and Expert (1, 1200) — Foundation excluded
guidedPracticeTests.expectedQuery: SELECT difficulty, COUNT(*) AS num_quests, AVG(xp_reward) AS mean_reward FROM quests WHERE difficulty IS NOT NULL GROUP BY difficulty HAVING AVG(xp_reward) > 200

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo Challenge — Difficulties with multiple quests

Same data. Write a query that returns just the difficulty names where there is more than one quest. One column called difficulty. Use HAVING COUNT(*) > 1.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between WHERE and HAVING to someone who has just learned GROUP BY. Use a quests-table example: write one query that demonstrates a row-level filter (WHERE) and one that demonstrates a bucket-level filter (HAVING), and explain why each filter belongs at its stage of the pipeline.

questions.questionHtml: Which clause filters buckets after GROUP BY has run?
options: HAVING
WHERE
FILTER
GROUP BY itself
questions.explanationHtml: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters the resulting buckets, and is the only clause where you can use aggregate functions (e.g. HAVING COUNT(*) > 1) as the condition.

questions.questionHtml: What is the correct on-the-page order of clauses in a SELECT query?
options: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT
SELECT, FROM, GROUP BY, WHERE, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT
SELECT, FROM, HAVING, GROUP BY, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT
SELECT, FROM, WHERE, HAVING, GROUP BY, ORDER BY, LIMIT
questions.correctAnswer: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT
questions.explanationHtml: Fixed grammar. The engine evaluates them in a slightly different order (FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT) but on the page the order above is the only valid one.

questions.questionHtml:
Using the quests table, what does this query return?

SELECT difficulty, COUNT(*) AS num
FROM quests
WHERE difficulty IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY difficulty
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;
options: Foundation 2
Foundation 2, Practitioner 1, Expert 1
Foundation 2, Practitioner 1, Expert 1, NULL 1
Nothing — no difficulty has 2 or more quests
questions.explanationHtml: WHERE drops the NULL-difficulty quest. GROUP BY makes three buckets: Foundation (2 rows), Practitioner (1 row), Expert (1 row). HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 keeps only Foundation. The result is a single row.

questions.questionHtml: You want "all difficulty categories where the average reward is over 200, looking only at quests that have been completed." Which query expresses this correctly?
options: SELECT difficulty, AVG(xp_reward) FROM quests WHERE completed_by IS NOT NULL GROUP BY difficulty HAVING AVG(xp_reward) > 200;
SELECT difficulty, AVG(xp_reward) FROM quests GROUP BY difficulty HAVING completed_by IS NOT NULL AND AVG(xp_reward) > 200;
SELECT difficulty, AVG(xp_reward) FROM quests WHERE completed_by IS NOT NULL AND AVG(xp_reward) > 200 GROUP BY difficulty;
SELECT difficulty, AVG(xp_reward) FROM quests HAVING completed_by IS NOT NULL GROUP BY difficulty WHERE AVG(xp_reward) > 200;
questions.correctAnswer: SELECT difficulty, AVG(xp_reward) FROM quests WHERE completed_by IS NOT NULL GROUP BY difficulty HAVING AVG(xp_reward) > 200;
questions.explanationHtml: Two filters at two stages: WHERE drops uncompleted quests before grouping, then HAVING drops difficulty buckets whose post-aggregation average is too low. Option 2 misuses HAVING (you cannot reference completed_by there because it isn't grouped or aggregated). Option 3 puts an aggregate in WHERE, which is invalid (aggregates don't exist yet at that pipeline stage). Option 4 has the clauses in an order the parser will reject.
